title: The pitch
summary: Sell the free build to the family with the plan and the priced list in hand, then stand through the cross-examination: they attack the budget line by line, never the choice, and every line survives with a reason or changes on the spot.
materials: the winning plan and the priced list from Build
whiteboard or a big sheet, for the money slide
the family, gathered for ten minutes

steps.title: Selling a plan you believe in
steps.body:
A pitch is a talk that asks for something. Yours asks the family to say yes to the build and open the cap, and a good pitch earns the yes the same way every good talk this season has: claim, reason, example. The claim is what you will build and who it is for. The reason is the groan it fixes, in your person's own words. The example is the plan itself, held up, pointed at, real.

The rules of the room, agreed before you start: the choice is yours, the budget is theirs to test. Nobody may say build something else. Anybody may say why does line four cost six dollars. That deal is what makes this a real pitch and not a performance: the questions will be honest, so the numbers must be too.

One more thing to carry in: the philosophy question of the week. What makes a gift good, the price or the thought? You are about to spend real money and three weeks of real work on one person. As you pitch, notice which of the two you are actually selling, because your recording ends with your answer.

Voice rules, same three as always: speak to the back wall, pause after the sentence that matters most, look at one person per sentence.

After the family votes on the build, one more round, and it turns the evening's own question back on you. You will have just defended a price list line by line, every number checked, every line worth what it costs. So tonight's motion is 'The thought behind a gift is worth more than the price', three rounds, either side, and you steelman the other side before you answer it. The list you defended is the evidence for whichever side you take.

steps.title: Build the two-minute pitch
steps.body:
Shape the pitch in five beats, and write one line for each on the whiteboard's corner before you practise.

The person and the groan: one sentence each, the groan in their words. The fix: name your build and say in one sentence what it does for them. The how: hold up the plan, point at the heart of it, then point at the scary part and say its plan B out loud; hiding the risk is what salespeople do, showing it is what engineers do. The money slide: draw it big, cap at the top, pay yourself first slice off the top next, spending number, total, and the gap between them. Say the slice line plainly: this much leaves first and is not for spending. The ask: say yes tonight and the shopping happens this weekend, so building starts on time.

Practise twice with a timer, out loud, plan in hand. Two minutes is the wall: past it, family attention wanders and pitches die politely. If you are over, cut description, never the money slide; the numbers are the part they came for.
checklist: The five beats are up: person and groan, fix, how with the scary part named, money slide, ask
The money slide shows cap, slice off the top, spending number, and total, all real
The scary part and its plan B are said out loud, not hidden
Two timed run-throughs landed under two minutes

steps.title: The cross-examination
steps.body:
Deliver the pitch to the gathered family, then open the floor with the line that starts every good budget fight: the numbers are yours to attack, the choice is mine to keep.

They go line by line down the priced list, and the steelman rule from debate weeks is strict here: before you answer any challenge, say it back so fairly that the challenger nods. Then, and only then, answer. Every challenged line has exactly two honest exits: it survives, because you give a reason with something real behind it, a price you checked, a part the plan truly needs; or it changes, right there, swapped or cut, and you say thank you, because they just saved your build money. Defending a line you secretly agree is weak is losing while sounding busy.

If a change happens, redo the total out loud on the money slide in front of everyone, and check it still fits under the spending number. Budgets move; the arithmetic moves with them, in public.

End by asking for the verdict, plainly: yes, or yes after these changes. Write the final total and any changed lines on the list, because that exact paper is what the weekend shopping runs on.
checklist: Every family challenge was said back fairly before I answered it
Each attacked line either survived with a real reason or changed on the spot
Any change got the total redone out loud on the money slide
The verdict is written on the list: yes, or yes with the named changes

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the two-minute pitch in one take, plan and money slide in frame. Keep the camera rolling for one cross-examination exchange: a family challenge, your steelman of it, and your answer. Close the recording with your answer to the question of the week: what makes a gift good, the price or the thought?
